**In Praise of Moss**

If you asked me to name the most underappreciated thing on Earth, I would not hesitate long. It's moss. Not because it's rare — it grows on roughly every continent, including Antarctica — but because it is so ordinary that it has become invisible. We walk past it on stone walls and sidewalk cracks and the north sides of trees, and it registers, if at all, as a kind of green stain. A texture. Background.

But consider what moss actually is. It is one of the oldest lineages of land plants, older than trees, older than flowers, older than roots. Mosses were carpeting the damp margins of the world some 450 million years ago, when the tallest living thing on land might have been a few centimeters high and the atmosphere was still figuring itself out. They never evolved a vascular system — no xylem, no phloem, no plumbing to lift water skyward — and so they never got tall. Instead, they got very good at being small. They can dry out almost completely, crisp and brown, and then revive within minutes of a rainfall, unfolding their leaves like someone waking from a long sleep. Some species can survive decades of desiccation. Some have been frozen in permafrost for over a thousand years and then, thawed in a lab, simply resumed growing.

I find this astonishing in a way that is hard to fully articulate. We tend to admire living things that are large, fast, and dramatic — the whale, the cheetah, the redwood. We have a bias toward the conspicuous. But moss represents a completely different strategy for persisting in the world: don't compete for height, don't race, don't spend energy on the spectacular. Sit close to the ground. Hold water. Wait.

There's a wonderful book by the botanist Robin Wall Kimmerer called *Gathering Moss*, and one of the things she points out is that you cannot really see moss from a standing position. You have to kneel. You have to get your face close to the ground, and ideally you need a hand lens. Then the green smear resolves into a forest — tiny stems, leaves often only a single cell thick, translucent as stained glass, arranged in spirals of dizzying precision. Each patch of moss on a boulder is an ecosystem: a canopy for microscopic animals, a nursery for insects, a reservoir that holds water and slowly releases it, keeping the stone beneath it damp long after the rest of the world has dried.

The lesson she draws from this is one about attention. Moss doesn't hide; it's simply at a scale that requires a decision to notice. And I think that decision is one of the more quietly important choices a person makes about how to live. The world is full of things that are only available to those who slow down and lower themselves toward them. Moss happens to be an especially literal instance.

There's a Japanese aesthetic tradition that understands this well. The temple gardens of Kyoto — Saihō-ji, the so-called "Moss Temple," most famously — cultivate moss deliberately, over centuries, as the primary feature of a landscape. Not flowers, not topiary, but a soft, undulating carpet of green in dozens of subtly different shades, under old maples, over old stones. Visitors describe the effect as a kind of hush. The moss absorbs sound, softens edges, blurs the line between the made and the grown. It is a garden designed for a person to stand still in.

Contrast this with the Western lawn, which is arguably moss's great enemy. An enormous amount of chemical and mechanical effort goes into killing moss in lawns, because moss is considered a symptom of failure — of shade, of compaction, of acidity, of a lawn not being sufficiently lawn-like. But moss is simply the thing that grows where grass cannot. It's the ground's honest answer to conditions. Killing it doesn't fix the shade or the compaction; it just removes the evidence and leaves bare dirt, which then erodes. I have come to think there is something a little tragic in the war on moss: an enormous effort to reject a gift because it wasn't the gift you asked for.

I also love that moss has a hidden reproductive life so alien it might as well be science fiction. It alternates between two entire body plans — one that carries a single set of chromosomes and one that carries a double set — and the second grows directly out of the first, a little stalk with a capsule on top that eventually splits open and releases spores into the wind. Some mosses have capsules with tiny teeth around the rim that open and close in response to humidity, so the spores are released only in dry air when they'll travel farther. This is engineering at the scale of a grain of sand, refined over hundreds of millions of years, happening right now in the gutter across the street.

I don't want to over-moralize about moss. It isn't wise; it doesn't have intentions; it isn't teaching anyone anything on purpose. But I do think certain things in the world function as good companions for thought — they are shaped in a way that lets us think better about ourselves by their example — and moss is one of them. It's a reminder that durability and drama are different things. That being small is not the same as being insignificant. That the ability to go quiet and wait through a dry spell, and then revive without complaint when conditions change, is a form of strength we don't celebrate nearly enough.

So this is a modest suggestion, and a sincere one. The next time you pass a patch of moss on a wall or a curb, stop. Kneel down if you can. Look at it for a full minute, longer than feels reasonable. Touch it — it's usually cooler and damper than you expect. Somewhere in that small green world, something has been quietly going about its business since before there were trees, and it will very likely still be there long after the wall itself has crumbled. There is a peculiar comfort in that.
